1.pericope_label: Remember, O LORD, what is come upon us: consider, and behold our reproach
debates: Why the chapter counts twenty-two verses without being alphabetic
Whom the orphans and the widowed mothers are
Which houses are meant by the second clause
outliers: Ellicott infers that the chapter was meant to be alphabetic and survives half finished, the prophet having written freely first and intended to bring it under the scheme afterwards
Clarke infers the opposite, that anything so technical was not thought proper by men in agony prostrating themselves for mercy
Keil and Delitzsch reject the readings that make the father the king and the mothers either the cities or the royal harem, and take both clauses as comparisons drawn from a Hebrew way of speaking
Gill records and rejects the reading that applies the whole chapter to the later church rather than to the people in Babylon
themes: Complaints not of evils feared but of evils felt
Help prepared the moment God is pleased to look
A great house passing to an unequal master
Orphans in the natural, civil and religious sense

4.pericope_label: We have drunken our water for money; our wood is sold unto us. Our necks are under persecution: we labour, and have no rest
debates: Whether the water and wood point to the besieged, the exiles or those left behind
Whether the necks carry a yoke or a pursuer
Whether the saying about the fathers pleads innocence
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch reject four historical applications of the verse and rest the whole force on the possessive pronouns
Keil and Delitzsch refuse to supply a yoke and reject attaching the phrase about the necks to the previous verse, since that destroys the symmetry
Calvin cites two Latin poets who blamed the crimes of ancestors and made their own generation innocent, and denies that the prophet means anything of the kind
Clarke distinguishes national judgments, which must fall in this life since nations as such cannot be punished in another, as the only sense in which children bear the sins of fathers
themes: Water sold where water is everywhere free
Enemies riding on the neck rather than following
A people that had lent and now begged
A double penalty borne by the later generation

8.pericope_label: Servants have ruled over us: there is none that doth deliver us out of their hand
debates: Who the servants that ruled were
Whether the word means sword or drought
Whether the skin was blackened or made to glow
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch reject four identifications of the servants and take the word of the conquerors, who ought rather to have served this people had it been faithful
Calvin reads drought rather than sword and asks what a sword has to do with a wilderness, saying those who chose the other sense cannot have regarded the context
Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both read the skin as glowing rather than blackened, since the word for oven denotes the fire in it rather than soot on it
Calvin makes the outrage sacrilege as well as disgrace, since the place named was the earthly dwelling chosen for the worship of the name of God
themes: Servants of servants rather than of kings
Bread fetched at the price of a life
A skin like a baker oven
A part named for the whole because it was holy

12.pericope_label: Princes are hanged up by their hand: the faces of elders were not honoured
debates: Whose hand hanged the princes
What the young men were made to carry
Whether the gate stands for justice or for society
outliers: Calvin argues that the princes were driven to lay violent hands on themselves, and wonders that the harsher sense never occurred to other interpreters
Keil and Delitzsch deny that the phrase means taken for the mill, and take the carrying of the portable hand-mill itself as the heaviest part of the labour
Keil and Delitzsch insist the gate was a place of social entertainment as well as of judgment, proving it from the parallel clause about music
Calvin rejects the old rendering that made the young men basely abused, since the word means to grind and the second half of the verse will not bear it
themes: A death chosen rather than suffered
Exposure that spares neither age nor dignity
Laws mute and barbarity worse than solitude
A people dispersed so that it should not combine

16.pericope_label: The crown is fallen from our head: woe unto us, that we have sinned!
debates: What the fallen crown stands for
How the confession here stands with the earlier saying about the fathers
Whether the verse about the mountain joins the one before it
outliers: Ellicott declines to narrow the crown to the temple or the city, calling it naturally symbolic of degradation
Calvin uses the confession to show that the earlier saying about the fathers did not exempt the living, since here the speaker condemns them and includes himself
Keil and Delitzsch read the fainting heart and the dim eyes as parallel, the sorrow of the soul and its expression in tears
Ellicott would render the animals jackals rather than foxes, haunting the ruins
themes: A crown worn at weddings as well as by kings
Hearts that faint where they had only grieved
Beasts walking where God had come down to dwell
A habitation ended and a throne enduring

19.pericope_label: Thou, O LORD, remainest for ever; thy throne from generation to generation
debates: What comfort the permanence of God yields here
Whether the expostulation is impatience
Why the closing verse is repeated in the manuscripts
outliers: Calvin observes that the parallel psalm infers the perpetuity of the church from the perpetuity of God, and holds that inference implied here though not drawn
Calvin holds that the prophet was relying on his own prophecies and deferring hope to the end of the seventy years, the complaint of length being made by human judgment
Calvin thinks the prayer was composed to outlast its author, dictated so that the faithful might use it after his death
Keil and Delitzsch report that the closing verse is repeated in many manuscripts so that the book may not end with the wrath of God, and hold that rightly understood it never required this
themes: A sanctuary in ruins and its owner unchanged
Eyes raised because nothing below stands still
Complaints deposited in the bosom of God
Hope glimmering like the morning star through clouds

21.pericope_label: Turn thou us unto thee, O LORD, and we shall be turned; renew our days as of old
debates: What kind of turning is prayed for
Whether the last verse states a fact, a condition or a question
Why the last verse is repeated in some copies
outliers: Calvin denies that repentance is meant and distinguishes an inward turning by the Spirit, a turning of feeling on our side, and an outward turning by which the favour of God becomes apparent
Ellicott renders the last particle unless, so that utter rejection is named only as the one impossible thing that could prevent renewal
Calvin rejects the reading that divides the verse conditionally, and thinks it was contrived because the plain sense seemed too harsh
Clarke reports one scholar who takes the particle as causal and another who holds that no good sense is possible unless the verse is read as a question
themes: A door closed on God by confining his power
Issues of death held in one hand
A prayer heard at the end of seventy years
A single word left standing in the oldest copy
